client: I've been feeling completely overwhelmed lately trying to keep my grades perfect while working 20 hours a week at the cafe. I know I should be able to handle this, but I keep having panic attacks whenever I think about my upcoming exams. Part of me wonders if talking about it will actually help, since I don't really have a choice about either responsibility.
therapist: I hear both determination and exhaustion in your voice as you describe this heavy load you're carrying. client:
Yeah, I guess there is some hope there... but it's buried under so much guilt. I feel like if I don't keep pushing myself to handle everything, I'm letting people down. My family depends on me, and the thought of saying no makes me feel like a terrible person. 

It's just hard to imagine another way when everyone expects so much from me. Even thinking about setting boundaries makes me anxious - like I'm being selfish or failing them somehow.
therapist: Your voice sounds both rushed and weary as you describe this heavy weight of expectations - I can hear how deeply this guilt and fear of disappointing others is affecting you. That tension between wanting to meet everyone's needs while also caring for yourself comes through so clearly. Let's gently examine what makes you feel that setting boundaries would mean you're failing them - what would you say to a friend in your situation?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I know logically that I'd tell a friend it's okay to set boundaries, but it feels different when it's me. There's this voice in my head saying if I don't do everything perfectly for everyone, I'm being selfish. I guess part of me worries people will think less of me if I say no sometimes.
therapist: Your voice sounds both urgent and strained as you describe this inner conflict - that gap between what you know logically and what you feel emotionally seems really painful right now. client: I know logically that people probably wouldn’t think less of me for setting limits, but emotionally it feels like I’m failing them if I don’t meet every expectation. It’s hard to shake the thought that I’ll be judged or seen as inadequate, even though I know that’s not entirely rational. I guess I just worry that if I start saying no, people will stop relying on me or valuing me.

client:

But at the same time, I'm so tired of performing all the time. It's exhausting pretending to be who I think people want me to be. I just don't know how to stop.

client:

therapist: Your voice sounds both rushed and tight as you describe this pattern of expecting rejection - I can hear how those rare positive moments get drowned out by the louder fear of being "found out." client: I don't know...those positive moments just feel like flukes, like the other person was just being polite or didn't see the real me yet. I guess it is exhausting, but stopping feels dangerous - like I'd be setting myself up for worse disappointment.
therapist: Your voice sounds both higher and more urgent as you describe this automatic discounting of positive moments - I can hear how protective that "don't count" reflex feels, even as it leaves you feeling isolated.
